methodological_rigor.justification: Large nationwide Korean NHIS-HEALS cohort (n=131,167) with clearly defined BP trajectory groups, landmark approach to reduce immortal time bias, cause-specific Cox models with extensive covariate adjustment, and multiple pre-specified sensitivity analyses (2/4/6-year exposure windows, 1-5 year lag times, ACC/AHA 2017 vs ESC 2024 vs JNC 7 thresholds). Proportional hazards assumption was tested (Schoenfeld p=0.485). Limitations appropriately acknowledged include residual confounding and lack of causal inference. Statistical approach is strong with competing risks handling and effect sizes plus CIs, though the attenuation under ACC/AHA 2017 thresholds needs careful interpretation.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: Individual prospective-style retrospective cohort derived from nationwide claims-linked health screening data classifies as Oxford LoE 2b. Clinical relevance is moderate: findings support proactive BP control and adherence with particular attention to colorectal and pancreatic cancer screening, but effect sizes are modest (aHR 1.16) and causality cannot be established. Not practice-changing but adds meaningful evidence informing clinical vigilance.

reporting_quality.justification: This observational cohort study adheres closely to STROBE: clear flow of exclusions (Supplementary Figure S2), pre-specified exposure definition, covariate justification, handling of competing risks, and sensitivity/subgroup analyses are well reported. Data availability is limited because NHIS-HEALS data are restricted and cannot be shared openly; access requires agreement with the Korean National Health Insurance Service. Code is not mentioned to be deposited.

novelty_literature.justification: Prior studies have examined hypertension-cancer links and prehypertension-cancer links separately (cited references 28-31). The novel contribution is examining BP trajectories (reversion, persistence, progression) from prehypertension rather than cross-sectional classification, combined with medication adherence stratification. This is a meaningful methodological extension but not a first-in-class or paradigm-shifting finding.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is clearly organized with well-structured methods, logical results flow, and an appropriately hedged discussion that acknowledges limitations and alternative explanations for subgroup findings. Tables and supplementary materials are referenced clearly. Minor grammatical issues ('could prove the need'), but overall the prose is precise and accessible.

key_strengths: Large nationwide cohort (n=131,167) with 10.7-year follow-up and uniform national health-screening criteria
Landmark approach and cause-specific Cox with competing risks to mitigate immortal time bias
Pre-specified sensitivity analyses across exposure windows, lag times, and BP guideline thresholds
Novel BP trajectory framing (reversion/persistence/progression) with medication adherence (MPR) stratification
Transparent reporting of discrepancy between ESC 2024 and ACC/AHA 2017 reclassification results
key_concerns: Effect sizes are modest (aHR 1.16 overall GI cancer) and claims-based ascertainment may introduce miscoding
Results under ACC/AHA 2017 guidelines were attenuated and non-significant, limiting external generalizability
Korean-only cohort may not generalize to other ethnic or screening contexts
NHIS-HEALS data are restricted-access; no analysis code deposited
Residual confounding (diet, H. pylori, family adenoma history) cannot be excluded
High-adherence subgroup showed unexpectedly elevated esophageal and pancreatic cancer risks suggesting unmeasured confounders
chief_reviewer.rationale: Methodologically solid nationwide cohort study with pre-specified sensitivity analyses and appropriately modest effect estimates; adds incremental mechanistic and clinical-vigilance insight rather than practice-changing evidence, supporting Tier 3 with minor revisions.
